t: Edge Impulse: What Edge Impulse Is and Why It Exists
title: Edge Impulse: What Edge Impulse Is and Why It Exists
description: Edge Impulse is a tinyML development platform founded in 2019 by Jan Jongboom and Zach Shelby. It exists because training a neural network on a workstation is only half the job: the model must then run inside the tight RAM, flash, and power budget of a microcontroller. The platform walks you through the full pipeline in one studio — collect sensor data, design an impulse (DSP feature-extraction block plus ML learn block), train, then export a portable C++ library that runs on Arduino, Nordic, ST, Espressif, and dozens of other targets, with no cloud dependency at deploy time.
key_facts: Founded 2019 by Jan Jongboom and Zach Shelby
Exports models as portable C++ libraries
Supports Arduino, Nordic, ST, Espressif targets
Free community tier for developers

t: Edge Impulse: The Impulse: DSP Block Plus Learn Block
title: Edge Impulse: The Impulse: DSP Block Plus Learn Block
description: Every Edge Impulse project is built around an impulse: a processing pipeline with two block types. The DSP (digital signal processing) block turns raw sensor samples into features — spectral analysis, MFCCs for audio, or flatten/image blocks for vision. The learn block is the neural network itself: classifier, regressor, anomaly detector (K-means), or object detection (FOMO). The studio shows estimated latency, RAM, and flash for each block combination before you train, so you can trade accuracy against the device budget deliberately.
key_facts: Impulse = DSP block + learn block
Learn blocks: classifier, regressor, anomaly, FOMO detection
Studio estimates latency/RAM/flash before training

t: Edge Impulse: Collecting and Labeling Sensor Data
title: Edge Impulse: Collecting and Labeling Sensor Data
description: Models are only as good as their data, so Edge Impulse treats acquisition as a first-class step: connect a board over serial or use the data-forwarder CLI to stream accelerometer, microphone, or camera samples straight into the project, then split them into training and test sets and label each window (e.g., 'idle', 'shake', 'tap'). The platform supports uploading existing datasets as CSV/WAV, and every sample keeps its metadata so experiments stay reproducible. Balanced classes and real-world noise in the training set are what separate a demo from a fieldable model.

t: Edge Impulse: Your First Impulse: Motion Classification
title: Edge Impulse: Your First Impulse: Motion Classification
description: The canonical first project is motion classification on an accelerometer: record idle, shake, and tap gestures, add a spectral-analysis DSP block, attach a small dense classifier, and train. Training runs in the cloud (or on your own machine with the enterprise runner) and returns accuracy plus a confusion matrix. One click exports the trained impulse as an Arduino library or generic C++ SDK; the included examples run inference on live sensor data and print the predicted class over serial. Typical result: a few tens of kilobytes of flash and single-digit millisecond inference.
key_facts: Spectral DSP + dense classifier is the starter recipe
Confusion matrix validates per-class quality
Export as Arduino library or C++ SDK

t: Edge Impulse: EON Compiler: Shrinking Models for MCUs
title: Edge Impulse: EON Compiler: Shrinking Models for MCUs
description: The EON Compiler is Edge Impulse's deployment optimizer: it takes the trained TensorFlow Lite model and compiles it to optimized C++ source, applying quantization (int8), operator fusion, and memory planning so the model fits microcontrollers with as little as tens of kilobytes of RAM. The EON Tuner goes further, sweeping DSP parameters and network architectures to find the best accuracy-per-byte trade for your target. Together they routinely cut RAM and flash by large factors versus a naive TFLite-Micro export, which is the difference between fitting on a Cortex-M4 and needing a bigger part.

int8 quantization plus operator fusion
EON Tuner sweeps architectures for accuracy-per-byte

t: Edge Impulse: DSP Feature Blocks: Spectral, MFCC, Image
title: Edge Impulse: DSP Feature Blocks: Spectral, MFCC, Image
description: Raw sensor data is rarely model-ready. Edge Impulse's DSP blocks do the heavy lifting: spectral analysis computes FFT-based features over sliding windows for vibration and motion; MFCC/MFE blocks extract mel-scale cepstral features for keyword spotting and audio events; the image block resizes and normalizes frames for FOMO object detection. Choosing window size and stride sets the trade between time resolution and compute cost, and the studio visualizes the resulting features so you can see class separation before training a single epoch.
key_facts: Spectral analysis for motion/vibration
MFCC/MFE for audio keyword spotting
Image block feeds FOMO detection

t: Edge Impulse: Anomaly Detection with K-Means
title: Edge Impulse: Anomaly Detection with K-Means
description: Not every problem has labeled failure examples. Edge Impulse's anomaly block clusters normal-operation features with K-means; at runtime, a sample far from every cluster centroid scores as anomalous. This is the workhorse for predictive maintenance: train on a healthy motor's vibration signature, deploy, and flag the bearing failure weeks before a human would hear it. The anomaly score is a single number, cheap to threshold on-device, and the studio shows the cluster map so you can sanity-check what 'normal' looks like.

Distance from centroids = anomaly score

t: Edge Impulse: Defensive Uses: On-Sensor Intrusion Sensing
title: Edge Impulse: Defensive Uses: On-Sensor Intrusion Sensing
description: tinyML's defensive value is locality: inference happens on the sensor, so raw data never traverses a network. Edge Impulse projects are used for tamper detection (classifying chassis vibration signatures of prying vs. normal handling), acoustic anomaly monitoring of server rooms, and air-quality or RF-environment sensing at the edge. Because the model runs on the microcontroller itself, a compromised network still cannot reach the raw sensor stream — the device only emits verdicts, and verdicts can be signed.
key_facts: Inference on-sensor keeps raw data off the network
Tamper and acoustic-anomaly classification
Devices emit signed verdicts, not raw streams

t: Edge Impulse: Integrating with Firmware: The C++ SDK
title: Edge Impulse: Integrating with Firmware: The C++ SDK
description: The exported C++ library drops into existing firmware: initialize the impulse once, then in your sensor loop fill the signal buffer, call run_classifier, and read the result struct with per-class scores and the anomaly value. The SDK has no OS dependency and no heap requirement beyond its static arena, so it ports to bare-metal, FreeRTOS, Zephyr, or Mbed with the same call pattern. Continuous-inference examples show the sliding-window pattern that keeps classification running while the main loop does other work.

t: Edge Impulse: Debugging: Feature Explorer and Live Classification
title: Edge Impulse: Debugging: Feature Explorer and Live Classification
description: When accuracy disappoints, Edge Impulse gives you the Feature Explorer: a 2D/3D projection of your dataset's feature space where misclassified points stand out visually, telling you whether the problem is bad data, bad features, or an underpowered model. Live classification streams real sensor data through the trained impulse in the browser, so you can wave the board and watch predictions update. The data-augmentation and DSP-parameter knobs are right there, closing the loop between 'it fails on this gesture' and a fixed pipeline.
key_facts: Feature Explorer visualizes class separation

Stage-level failure attribution

t: Edge Impulse: FOMO: Object Detection on Tiny Cameras
title: Edge Impulse: FOMO: Object Detection on Tiny Cameras
description: FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects) is Edge Impulse's object-detection architecture for microcontrollers: instead of predicting bounding boxes, it predicts object centroids on a coarse grid, which slashes compute while still counting and localizing objects. It runs at multiple frames per second on a Cortex-M7 with a small camera — enough for people counting, pallet detection, or perimeter presence sensing at the edge, with no video ever leaving the device. That last property is the defensive point: the camera's raw feed stays on the chip.
key_facts: FOMO predicts centroids, not boxes
Multi-FPS on Cortex-M7 class parts
Raw video stays on-device

t: Edge Impulse: Air-Gapped and Enterprise Deployment
title: Edge Impulse: Air-Gapped and Enterprise Deployment
description: Defense and industrial users cannot always phone home. Edge Impulse supports this with downloadable C++ exports (no runtime cloud call), on-premise training runners, and SSO/audit enterprise tiers. The exported library is fully offline: once flashed, the device classifies forever without connectivity. For fleets, the model-versioning workflow lets you A/B new impulses across device groups and roll back by flashing the previous export — standard practice for fielded sensor networks.

t: Edge Impulse: Testing: From Studio Metrics to Field Trials
title: Edge Impulse: Testing: From Studio Metrics to Field Trials
description: A responsible tinyML workflow tests in layers: studio accuracy and confusion matrix first, then the EON-compiled model's on-device metrics (latency, RAM, flash measured on the real target, not estimated), then a field trial where the device logs predictions alongside ground truth for days. Edge Impulse's testing tab automates the first layer and the SDK's logging examples support the last. The number that matters is field accuracy on unseen conditions — temperature drift, battery sag, and mounting differences all move the needle.

t: Edge Impulse: Real-World Pattern: Predictive Maintenance Node
title: Edge Impulse: Real-World Pattern: Predictive Maintenance Node
description: A complete defensive-industrial pattern: a vibration sensor node on a pump motor, running an Edge Impulse impulse with spectral DSP and an anomaly block. It learns the healthy signature during commissioning, then reports a daily health score and immediate alerts on anomaly spikes — all computed on a $10-class MCU, with a LoRa radio sending only the score. Maintenance crews get weeks of warning on bearing wear, and the raw vibration stream never leaves the machine room.

t: Edge Impulse: Mastery: The Road to Field-Grade tinyML
title: Edge Impulse: Mastery: The Road to Field-Grade tinyML
description: Mastery means thinking in budgets: every project starts from the device's RAM/flash/latency/power envelope and works backward to the model, not the reverse. Advanced practitioners co-design the DSP and network with the EON Tuner, validate with field soak logs, version models like firmware, and monitor drift — retraining when the world changes. The frontier is sensor fusion (audio plus motion plus vision in one impulse) and on-device adaptation, but the discipline stays the same: measure on the target, test in the field, and never trust a studio number alone.
key_facts: Budget-first design: device envelope before model
Version models like firmware; monitor drift
Signed model cards: hash, recipe, soak report
